newsitem.title: UK: Labour Wirral swing seen unlikely in national poll.
newsitem.headline: Labour Wirral swing seen unlikely in national poll.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party is still on course for a comfortable victory in the imminent general election, but cannot bank on a repeat of the massive 18 percent swing in its favour seen in Thursday's Wirral South by-election, leading political analysts said on Friday.

Labour won the by-election with a majority of 7,888 votes, reversing a Conservative majority of 8,183 at the last election in 1992. The result leaves the government with a minority in parliament with 322 seats, one fewer than all the other parties combined.
"Labour's lead is holding up in concrete terms, but by-election results should be treated carefully because they are exaggerated," said Neil Carter, lecturer in politics at the University of York.
"Every by-election the Conservatives lost up to 1992, was won back in the general election in that year."

Voters in Wirral South, a traditional "middle England" area which should be solid Conservative territory, indulged in the traditional British habit of making a by-election protest, but their natural allegiance would reassert itself for the general election, the experts said.
Prime Minister John Major must hold a national election by May 22 and the most heavily-tipped date is May 1.

"Motivation in a general election is different. People are voting for a government, not someone to represent them in parliament. I would not expect a repetition of the Wirral result in the general election," said Eric Shaw, senior lecturer in politics at the University of Stirling.
David Carlton, lecturer in politics at the University of Warwick, has been a lonely voice among British polling experts, until now predicting a small Conservative majority in the general election.

"The turnout was 73 percent, it was good, but not as good as the media made it out to be. If the turnout had been over 80 percent then a swing of 18 percent would have been extremely significant," said Carlton.
"I still see evidence that there may be a lower turnout at the general election than previously. I shall be changing my prediction to a hung parliament."
In the 1992 election, over 82 percent turned out to vote.
Colin Rallings, reader in politics at the University of Plymouth, said he was surprised by the extent of the swing.
He said opinion polls which have been predicting a strong Labour lead were often thought to under-represent the Conservative vote, but the Wirral result indicated otherwise.
"The business of hidden Tories and non-voters (in opinion polls) does not hold water any more," he said.

A national opinion poll carried out by polling organisation NOP and published by Reuters on Tuesday gave Labour a 20-point lead. Other opinion polls have also suggested a large majority for the opposition.
